planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; self-incompatible and needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar nearby.

directions: Tonda Pacifica was bred at Oregon State University from a cross of the celebrated Italian cultivar Tonda Gentile delle Langhe and an OSU breeding selection, then released in 2010 as a named commercial cultivar rather than pure breeding stock. It produces a smaller, more yield-efficient tree than the old industry standard Barcelona, bearing smaller nuts with an unusually high kernel percentage and few defects that suit the blanched-kernel, chocolate, and baking trade. Like Barcelona it remains susceptible to Eastern Filbert Blight, so growers in blight-prone regions should pair it with a resistant rootstock or maintain a fungicide program rather than counting on Tonda Pacifica's own disease tolerance. It also carries breeding significance as the female parent, crossed with Santiam, of the EFB-resistant OSU release McDonald.

common_name: Ratoli Hazelnut (Spanish Eastern Filbert Blight Resistance Source)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; needs a compatible cross-pollinating cultivar, since hazelnuts will not set a crop on their own pollen.

directions: Ratoli is a traditional Catalan hazelnut landrace long grown in the Reus-Tarragona region of northeastern Spain, an area that accounts for the great majority of Spanish hazelnut production. Its lasting importance to modern growers comes from a single dominant resistance gene to Eastern Filbert Blight, mapped to a different chromosome location than the Gasaway-derived resistance used in most Pacific Northwest breeding, which makes Ratoli valuable for diversifying the genetic sources of blight resistance in new cultivars. Rutgers University drew on this Ratoli-derived resistance in developing its blight-resistant release Somerset, which has shown no blight infection in New Jersey field trials. Ratoli itself remains a minor cultivar grown mostly in its traditional Catalan homeland and used elsewhere chiefly as breeding and resistance-screening germplasm rather than as a widely planted orchard variety.
sources: Rutgers New Jersey Agricultural Experiment Station

common_name: Kintzel Chinese Chestnut (Historic Ohio Blight-Resistant Selection, Parent of Jenny)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in late winter to early spring in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; a second, genetically distinct Chinese chestnut cultivar is needed nearby for pollination.

directions: Kintzel is an old Ohio Chinese chestnut selection, documented under the breeding designations Byron 1-1 and 1-2 in a 1962 Northern Nut Growers Association Nutshell article, and long valued among nut-tree collectors for combining genuine resistance to chestnut blight with excellent winter cold hardiness. Its most lasting legacy is as the seed parent of Jenny, a tall, early-ripening open-pollinated selection chosen by breeder J.M. Nave and since evaluated in Missouri chestnut trials, which has been distributed far more widely than Kintzel itself. Kintzel is rarely offered by name in the nursery trade today, surviving mainly in historic breeding records and in specialty nut-tree collections, while gardeners wanting its blight resistance and hardiness in a currently available tree are more likely to find its offspring Jenny. Space trees widely to accommodate a broad mature canopy typical of Chinese chestnut selections.
sources: Northern Nut Growers Association — The Nutshell (1962)
University of Missouri Center for Agroforestry

common_name: Lady of Fortune Daylily (Historic Parent of Elegant Candy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun; established clumps need only routine watering and division every three to four years.

directions: Registered in 1992, Lady of Fortune is a tetraploid daylily bearing single, cream-to-ivory blend flowers with a soft yellow-green throat on scapes reaching roughly two feet, blooming in the mid-to-late part of the daylily season. It carries lasting breeding significance as the seed parent, crossed with tetraploid Janice Brown, of Patrick Stamile's fragrant 1995 introduction Elegant Candy. Grow it in average, well-drained soil in full sun and divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep bloom production strong, exactly as with any modern tetraploid daylily.

common_name: Exotic Candy Daylily (Fragrant Parent of Huckleberry Candy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun; deadhead spent scapes to support the reliable rebloom this cultivar is known for.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 1995 from a cross of Wineberry Candy and tetraploid Janice Brown, Exotic Candy bears very fragrant, ruffled, round light-pink flowers over four inches across with a dark red-rose eyezone and green throat, opening midseason with dependable rebloom on dormant-foliage clumps. It went on to become one of the two parents, crossed with Magnificent Rainbow, of Stamile's 1998 introduction Huckleberry Candy, passing along its fragrance and crisp eyezone pattern to the next generation of the Candy breeding line. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Magnificent Rainbow Daylily (Lavender Bicolor Parent of Huckleberry Candy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun; established dormant-foliage clumps need only routine watering and periodic division.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 1995 from a cross of Always Afternoon and tetraploid Priscilla's Rainbow, Magnificent Rainbow bears large, six-inch lavender bicolor flowers with gray-blue overtones and an extended green throat on a comparatively low, dormant-foliage plant. It carries breeding significance as one of the two parents, crossed with Exotic Candy, of the 1998 introduction Huckleberry Candy, contributing its large flower size and watermark eye pattern to that later Candy-series cultivar. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years to sustain strong flowering.

common_name: Rock Solid Daylily (Fragrant Parent of Precious Candy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun; deadhead spent scapes through the season to sustain its heavy rebloom.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 2002 from a cross of Inner Destiny and Francois Verhaert, Rock Solid is a very fragrant tetraploid daylily bearing cream flowers nearly five inches across, marked with a plum-violet eye and edge over a green throat, opening early-to-midseason on well-branched scapes carrying more than thirty buds with reliable rebloom. It later became one of the two parents, crossed with Zahadoom, of Stamile's 2006 introduction Precious Candy, passing on its crisp eye-and-edge pattern to that later selection. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Zahadoom Daylily (Fragrant Parent of Precious Candy)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in full sun; semi-evergreen foliage benefits from a protective mulch at the colder edge of its range.

directions: Registered by Patrick Stamile in 2002, Zahadoom is a very fragrant, semi-evergreen tetraploid daylily bearing light brown-lavender flowers around five and a half inches across with a blue-purple eye and edge above a green throat, opening early-to-midseason. It carries breeding significance as one of the two parents, crossed with Rock Solid, of the 2006 introduction Precious Candy, contributing its distinctive eye-and-edge color pattern to that later Candy-series selection. Grow it in full sun in average, well-drained soil and divide congested clumps every three to four years to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Golden Supreme American Persimmon (Heavy-Cropping Parent of Elmo)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in full sun in any well-drained to average soil, and site a second American persimmon nearby, since Golden Supreme is a female clone and needs a male tree within pollinating range for a reliable crop.

directions: Golden Supreme is an older American persimmon clone of garden origin, grown for its bright orange, round fruit and consistently heavy annual cropping on a female tree. Ripening around mid-October, the fruit must fully soften after frost before its astringency fades, and while some growers rate its flavor as merely good rather than exceptional compared with named selections like Early Golden or Yates, its dependable yield has kept it in cultivation. Golden Supreme carries lasting breeding significance as one of the two parents, hand-pollinated with Garretson by Illinois hobbyist Jim Claypool, of the well-regarded modern selection Elmo. Give it the same deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and minimal care that other American persimmons need, and expect the tree's deep taproot to make it drought-tolerant once established.
